idiom_name: one reader per payload: select by name, default what is absent, ignore the rest
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: give every external payload exactly one reader - a dedicated mapper or DTO factory that selects the elements it needs by name or path, supplies an explicit default for each optional element, and never enumerates the payload as a whole, so unknown data is never visited and therefore never fails. Keep the normalised result in a DTO so the rest of the system depends on your model rather than on the wire shape, and do not let a second ad-hoc reader of the same payload appear elsewhere. Publish the consumed subset (the reader plus its tests) to the producer as a consumer-driven contract, and keep a deliberate distinction between "absent" (use the default) and "present but invalid" (fail fast).
code_sketch:
payload = parse(body)                       # generic tree (dict/map/JsonNode)
node    = payload.get('order', {})          # named selection, not whole-document binding
order = Order(
    id       = node['id'],                  # required: still fails fast when missing
    total    = node.get('total', 0),        # absent -> explicit default
    currency = node.get('currency', 'EUR'), # anything else (new fields) is ignored
)
pitfalls: Centralisation is a discipline, not a structure: several ad-hoc reads of the same payload reintroduce exactly the coupling the pattern removes.
Defaults must be explicit and documented; an accidental default turns a producer regression into plausible but wrong data.
Tolerance for added fields is not tolerance for removed, retyped or repurposed fields - those still need an explicit versioning path.

Formats with implicit presence (proto3 scalars without an explicit optional label) cannot separate an absent field from its zero value, so the default silently masks "the producer stopped sending it" - track presence explicitly wherever that distinction carries meaning.

Granting tolerance as a global deserialiser switch (disabling FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES for the whole mapper) also silences misspelled and hostile field names; scope it to the one payload type or call site, as Kubernetes does with per-request field validation.

A tolerant reader that round-trips the payload back to the producer destroys the fields it never read: Kubernetes documented typed clients dropping newer-schema fields when writing a custom resource against an older CRD version.
